summary: Defines a Router Advertisement option that explicitly identifies Provisioning Domains (PvDs), consistent sets of network configuration information. This lets hosts that use several networks at once, such as broadband and cellular, manage each properly.

eli5.summary: If your phone has two ways onto the internet, each one comes with its own set of rules. This labels each set of rules.

questions: how do hosts discover pvd names
what is the pvd option in router advertisements
what is the well-known pvd uri
how do hosts fetch pvd additional information
subtitle: A Router Advertisement option that gives each set of network settings a name, so a device on several networks can keep them apart.

tldr.problem: A host connected to several networks, or to a router offering several uplinks, receives configuration (addresses, DNS servers, routes) that it cannot reliably tell apart or tie to the network that provided it.
tldr.mechanism: A new Router Advertisement option, the PvD Option, carries a PvD ID (a fully qualified domain name) that labels all the configuration in that advertisement. It can also point to a JSON document, fetched over HTTPS from a well-known URI, with extra information about the network.
tldr.outcome: PvD-aware hosts can keep configurations separate and pick among them per connection, while hosts that do not know the option simply ignore it. The option does not improve Neighbor Discovery security.

today: RFC 8801 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2020, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the PvD Option and the PvD Additional Information format.

sections.title: Why Name a Provisioning Domain
sections.content:
A Provisioning Domain (PvD), as defined in RFC 7556, is a consistent set of network configuration information: source addresses, DNS configuration, proxy configuration, gateway addresses and similar properties that are traditionally tied to one network interface. Most PvDs today are discovered implicitly, from the Router Advertisements a host receives on an interface.

RFC 7556 also describes Explicit PvDs, but does not say how to discover several of them on one network. This RFC fills that gap. It identifies a PvD with a fully qualified domain name called a PvD ID, carried in a new option in the Router Advertisement (RA) message of RFC 4861.

That allows two things: several PvDs on a single interface (for example a router offering access to two different Internet service providers), and Additional Information describing the properties of a network. The RFC's own example is a home with both a cellular and a broadband provider, where a video application might choose the cellular network if it offers free high-quality streaming while other traffic uses broadband.
sections.eli5: Imagine a house with two mail slots from two different delivery companies. A name tag on each slot lets you tell which company's rules apply to each letter.

sections.title: The PvD Option
sections.content:
The PvD Option is an RA option of Type 21. Its main parts are:

  • Length: the length in units of 8 octets, covering the option header, any inner RA message header and the options inside it.
  • H-flag (HTTP): some PvD Additional Information is available over HTTP over TLS.
  • L-flag (Legacy): the PvD is associated with IPv4 information assigned using DHCPv4.
  • R-flag: a full Router Advertisement message header follows the option header after padding to the next 64-bit boundary.
  • Delay (4 bits): used to randomize the timing of HTTP queries. Sequence Number (16 bits): changes when new Additional Information is available.
  • PvD ID FQDN: the name, encoded in DNS format, with no name compression allowed. Zero padding then reaches the next 8-octet boundary.

After that come zero or more ordinary RA options. Placing them inside the PvD Option means hosts that are not PvD-aware ignore them, because they do not recognize the option code. The 9 reserved bits MUST be zero when sent and are ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: It is a label stuck onto a message. The label has the name of the network, a few yes-or-no switches, and room to tuck in extra notes that only label-readers will see.

sections.title: Router and Host Behavior
sections.content:
A router MAY include one PvD Option in an RA but MUST NOT include more than one, and a PvD Option MUST NOT contain another PvD Option. To offer several PvDs, a router MUST send several RAs. RAs from different link-local source addresses create distinct Implicit PvDs when no PvD Option is present, while several Explicit PvDs MAY share one link-local source address. If options would push an RA past the link MTU, the PvD Option header MUST be repeated in every RA sent.

A PvD-aware host MUST associate each RA and everything derived from it (addresses made from a Prefix Information Option, routes, DNS servers) with the Explicit PvD named by the first PvD Option, or with the Implicit PvD identified by interface and router address otherwise. Extra PvD Options are ignored. PvD IDs are compared case-insensitively. A host or application MAY then use just a subset of PvDs for address selection, name resolution or routing, and a constrained device may deliberately use only one.

The RFC also covers how other configuration is attached to PvDs:

  • DHCPv6: stateless items go with all PvDs on the interface whose RA has the O-flag; stateful assignments go with the PvD whose RA has the M-flag and a matching prefix.
  • DHCPv4: goes to the single Explicit PvD that sets the L-flag, otherwise to all Implicit PvDs on that interface.
  • Tethering: a host sharing its upstream connection SHOULD pass the same PvD ID and related values in the RAs it sends downstream.
  • DNS: servers SHOULD be tied to their PvD, and queries sent from an address provisioned for that PvD.
sections.eli5: Your device sorts every setting into the folder named on its label. When it needs to go online, it uses just one folder at a time so the rules from different networks never get tangled.

sections.title: Fetching the Additional Information
sections.content:
When the H-flag is set, a host MAY fetch the Additional Information with an HTTP-over-TLS GET to https://<PvD-ID>/.well-known/pvd, using the media type application/pvd+json. It MUST NOT do so when the H-flag is not set. The host MUST check that the server certificate has a DNS-ID equal to the PvD ID, and if that fails it closes the connection and treats the PvD as having no Additional Information. DNS resolution, certificate checks and the request itself MUST all use the configuration of that PvD, and the host SHOULD use a temporary address to fetch it.

The host remembers the last Sequence Number seen. When an RA for the same PvD arrives with a different number, or the information expires, the old information is deprecated. To avoid everyone querying at once, an update after a Sequence Number change waits a random time between zero and 2^(10 + Delay) milliseconds; with a Delay of 1 that is between 0 and 2048 milliseconds. Fetching on expiry uses a uniformly random time in the interval [(B-A)/2, B], where A is the fetch time and B the expiry.

Hosts MUST rate-limit requests. The RFC recommends at least 10 seconds between requests for the same PvD, and no more than five requests in total on a network within 10 seconds. After a failure (a certificate error, an HTTP error or invalid JSON) the host MUST NOT ask for that PvD ID again during the attachment, and after 10 or more failures it MUST stop requesting any PvD information on that network.

The network operator, for its part, MUST make a valid object available to all hosts when the H-flag is set, even behind a captive portal. Routers SHOULD increment the Sequence Number by one when a new object is available, wrapping to zero.
sections.eli5: If the label says there is a booklet about the network, your device asks for it politely, checks that the booklet really comes from the network's owner, and waits a random moment so a thousand devices do not all knock at once.

sections.title: The Additional Information JSON
sections.content:
The Additional Information is a JSON object restricted to the I-JSON profile. It carries data too large or not critical enough for an RA option. Three keys are mandatory, and an object missing any of them, or whose expiry is already past, MUST be ignored:

  • identifier: the PvD ID FQDN, which MUST match the one in the PvD Option.
  • expires: the date after which the object is no longer valid.
  • prefixes: an array of IPv6 prefixes valid for this PvD.

Two optional keys are defined: dnsZones (DNS zones searchable and accessible) and noInternet (true when the PvD is restricted). Every prefix in every Prefix Information Option in the RA MUST be covered by one of the listed prefixes, otherwise the information is treated as a misconfiguration and MUST NOT be used.

Unknown keys MUST be ignored. Private-use or experimental keys go in a sub-dictionary, for example vendor-foo, so they cannot collide with registered keys.
sections.eli5: The booklet is a short card with the network's name, an expiry date and a list of address ranges it owns. Anything on the card your device does not understand, it just skips.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
This RFC does not improve the Neighbor Discovery security model. Its check only confirms that the owner of the PvD ID authorizes its use with the prefix the router advertises. Section 4.4 notes that an adversarial router would need IPv6-to-IPv6 Network Prefix Translation (NPTv6) to get around the prefix check, and that the check gives reasonable assurance against misconfiguration but does not stop a hostile network access provider from advertising incorrect information. The server providing the JSON SHOULD check whether the client address is inside the listed prefixes and SHOULD return a 403 response if not.

Because absolute expiry times can be skewed by clocks, they MUST NOT be used for security-sensitive decisions. An attacker sending RAs could also try to make hosts open TLS connections to arbitrary servers, a form of denial-of-service amplification. The rate limits and the stop-after-failures rules in the previous section are the required mitigation.

On privacy, hosts SHOULD use a temporary IPv6 address, SHOULD NOT send a User-Agent header or cookie, and MUST use the PvD's own DNS servers so the name of the information server is not leaked onto another network. To avoid revealing which PvD IDs a host trusts, it SHOULD fetch information for all eligible PvD IDs on a network or for none.
sections.eli5: The label proves the network's name belongs to its owner, but it cannot protect you from a router that is out to trick you. So your device asks politely, shares very little about itself, and gives up if something looks fishy.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA removed the 'reclaimable' tag for value 21 (the PvD Option) in the IPv6 Neighbor Discovery Option Formats registry and added the pvd suffix to the Well-Known URIs registry. It also created two registries: Additional Information PvD Keys, managed by Expert Review, and PvD Option Flags, which reserves bit positions 0 to 11, with future assignments needing Standards Action.

Bits 0, 1 and 2 are assigned to the H-flag, L-flag and R-flag. The RFC also registers the media type application/pvd+json, whose encoding considerations are identical to those of application/json.
sections.eli5: The rule book gets new entries so everyone uses the same labels: the option number, the web address ending, and the name for the booklet's file type.

viz.caption: FIXED PART OF THE PVD OPTION (RFC 8801)

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Option length in units of 8 octets.

fields.name: H
fields.desc: Additional Information is available over HTTP over TLS.

fields.name: L
fields.desc: PvD is associated with DHCPv4 information.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Must be zero when sent; ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Delay
fields.desc: Randomizes HTTP queries by up to 2^(10 + Delay) milliseconds.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Changes when new Additional Information is available.
